units.title: Hello, Julia!
units.summary: Write your first Julia program, print text and numbers, and use Julia as a calculator.

lesson.md: A Julia program is a text file that ends in `.jl`. Julia runs it from top to bottom, one line after another. The function `println` prints a value and then starts a new line.

lesson.code:
println("Hello, World!")
println("I am learning Julia.")
lesson.output:
Hello, World!
I am learning Julia.

lesson.md: Text in double quotes, like `"Hello"`, is a **string**. The parentheses after `println` hold the value to print. Write no space between `println` and `(`, or Julia reports an error.

`print` prints a value without starting a new line, so the next output continues on the same line. You can also pass several values, separated by commas. Julia prints them one after another, with no space in between.

lesson.code:
print("Hello, ")
print("Julia")
println("!")
println("a", "b", "c")
println("Age: ", 30)

lesson.md: Numbers are written without quotes. Julia knows the usual operators: `+` adds, `-` subtracts, `*` multiplies and `/` divides. `^` raises a number to a power, so `2^3` is `2 * 2 * 2`.

lesson.code:
println(2 + 3)
println(10 - 4)
println(6 * 7)
println(7 / 2)
println(2^3)
println((1 + 2) * 4)

lesson.md: Julia follows the rules of math: `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`. So `1 + 2 * 4` is `9`. Use parentheses to change the order: `(1 + 2) * 4` is `12`.

`/` always gives a number with a decimal point, even when the result is whole: `10 / 2` is `5.0`. `div(7, 2)` divides and drops the rest, which gives `3`. `%` gives the rest (the remainder) of a division: `7 % 2` is `1`.

lesson.code:
println(10 / 2)
println(div(7, 2))
println(7 % 2)

lesson.md: A line that starts with `#` is a **comment**. Julia ignores it. Programmers use comments to leave notes for the people who read the code.

lesson.code:
# println("hidden")
println("visible")

card: `println("Hi")` prints and starts a new line

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables, meet Int64, Float64, String and Bool, and put values into text with $.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create it with `=`: the name on the left, the value on the right. After that, you can use the name instead of the value.

lesson.code:
name = "Ana"
age = 30
println(name)
println(age + 1)

lesson.md: You can give a variable a new value at any time. The new value replaces the old one. A variable can even be used to calculate its own new value: `points = points + 5`. The short form is `points += 5`. The same works with `-=`, `*=` and `/=`.

lesson.code:
points = 10
points = points + 5
println(points)
points += 1
println(points)
points *= 2
println(points)

lesson.md: Every value has a **type**. Whole numbers like `42` are `Int64`. Numbers with a decimal point like `2.5` are `Float64`. Text is a `String`, and the values `true` and `false` are `Bool`. The function `typeof` tells you the type of a value.

lesson.code:
println(typeof(42))
println(typeof(2.5))
println(typeof("hi"))
println(typeof(true))

lesson.md: Inside a string, `$` followed by a variable name inserts the value of the variable. For a calculation, put it in parentheses after the `$`: `$(age + 1)`. This is called **interpolation**. A name can contain `!`, so `"$name!"` looks for a variable `name!`. Write `"$(name)!"` instead.

lesson.code:
name = "Ben"
age = 25
println("$name is $age years old.")
println("Next year: $(age + 1)")
lesson.output:
Ben is 25 years old.
Next year: 26

lesson.md: `parse(Int, "42")` reads a whole number from a string. `Int` is the usual short name for `Int64`. `Float64(3)` turns a whole number into a `Float64`, and `string(7)` turns a number into a `String`.

lesson.code:
n = parse(Int, "42")
println(n + 1)
x = Float64(3)
println(x)
println(typeof(string(7)))

lesson.md: A number in quotes is a string. `"5" + 1` is an error, because Julia does not add text and numbers. Write `parse(Int, "5") + 1` instead.

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Join, repeat, measure and search text, and read single characters from a string.

lesson.md: You already know strings and interpolation with `$`. Julia has many more tools for text. The operator `*` joins two strings into one. This is called **concatenation**.

lesson.code:
first_name = "Ada"
last_name = "Lovelace"
full = first_name * " " * last_name
println(full)

lesson.md: `^` repeats a string: `"ab"^3` is `"ababab"`. The function `length` counts the characters of a string.

lesson.code:
println("ha"^3)
println("-"^10)
println(length("Julia"))

lesson.md: Use `*` to join strings, not `+`. `"a" + "b"` is an error in Julia.

`uppercase` and `lowercase` give a new string in capital or small letters. `occursin(part, text)` checks if `part` appears in `text` and gives `true` or `false`. `startswith` and `endswith` check the beginning and the end of a string.

lesson.code:
word = "Julia"
println(uppercase(word))
println(lowercase(word))
println(occursin("li", word))
println(occursin("x", word))
println(startswith(word, "Ju"))

lesson.md: `replace` swaps one part of a string for another. You write the old and the new part with `=>` between them. The original string does not change: `replace` gives you a new one.

lesson.code:
s = "I like cats"
println(replace(s, "cats" => "dogs"))
println(s)
lesson.output:
I like dogs
I like cats

lesson.md: `s[1]` gives the first character of `s`. In Julia, counting starts at **1**, not at 0. `s[end]` is the last character, and `s[2:4]` gives the characters 2 to 4 as a new string. A single character has the type `Char` and is written in single quotes, like `'J'`.

lesson.code:
s = "Julia"
println(s[1])
println(s[end])
println(s[2:4])
println(typeof(s[1]))

lesson.md: Strings use double quotes and characters use single quotes. `'Hi'` is an error, because a `Char` holds exactly one character.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program choose with if, elseif and else, compare values, and combine conditions with && and ||.

lesson.md: An `if` block runs code only when a condition is `true`. The block ends with the keyword `end`. The code inside is usually indented by four spaces. Julia does not need the spaces, but they make the code easier to read.

lesson.code:
temperature = 30
if temperature > 25
    println("It is hot.")
end
println("Done.")

lesson.md: Comparisons give a `Bool`. `==` checks if two values are equal, and `!=` checks if they are different. `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare sizes. Do not confuse `==` with `=`, which stores a value. You can also chain comparisons: `1 < x < 10` checks both sides at once.

lesson.code:
x = 7
println(x == 7)
println(x != 7)
println(x >= 10)
println(1 < x < 10)

lesson.md: `else` runs when the condition is `false`. `elseif` checks another condition. Julia tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is `true`.

lesson.code:
score = 72
if score >= 90
    println("Excellent")
elseif score >= 60
    println("Passed")
else
    println("Try again")
end

lesson.md: `&&` means **and**: both sides must be `true`. `||` means **or**: at least one side must be `true`. `!` turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.

lesson.code:
age = 20
has_ticket = true
if age >= 18 && has_ticket
    println("Welcome")
end
println(age < 12 || age > 65)
println(!has_ticket)

lesson.md: For a short choice between two values, write `condition ? a : b`. This is called the **ternary operator**. If the condition is `true`, the result is `a`, otherwise `b`. Julia needs the spaces around `?` and `:`.

lesson.code:
n = 5
kind = n % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd"
println("$n is $kind")

lesson.md: A condition must be a `Bool`. In Julia, `if 1` is an error, unlike in some other languages.

exercises.prompt: What does this print?
exercises.code:

    println("medium")

    println("small")
end
exercises.explain: `15 > 20` is `false`, but `15 > 10` is `true`, so the `elseif` block runs.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for and while, count with ranges like 1:5 and 10:-2:0, and control loops with break and continue.

lesson.md: A `for` loop repeats code for every value in a sequence. `1:5` is a **range**: the numbers from 1 to 5, both included. In each round, the loop variable `i` takes the next value `in` the range. Like `if`, the loop ends with `end`.

lesson.code:
for i in 1:3
    println(i)
end

lesson.md: A range can have a step in the middle: `start:step:stop`. `1:2:7` counts in steps of 2, and with a negative step like `9:-3:1` the range counts down.

lesson.code:
for i in 1:2:7
    println(i)
end
for i in 9:-3:1
    println(i)
end

lesson.md: A `for` loop works with other sequences, too. With a string, the loop visits every character.

lesson.code:
for c in "abc"
    println(uppercase(c))
end

lesson.md: To add up numbers, create a variable before the loop and change it inside the loop. At the top level of a script file, you must write `global` in front of such a change. Inside a function, which you meet in the next unit, you do not need `global`.

lesson.code:
total = 0
for i in 1:4
    global total += i
end
println(total)

lesson.md: Without `global`, Julia prints a warning and then stops with an error. Inside the loop, `total` counts as a new variable that has no value yet.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is `true`. Make sure that something inside the loop changes the condition, or the loop never ends.

lesson.code:
n = 3
while n > 0
    println(n)
    global n -= 1
end
println("Go!")

lesson.md: `break` leaves a loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one. Here, `continue` skips the even numbers, and `break` stops the loop after 7.

lesson.code:
for i in 1:10
    if i % 2 == 0
        continue
    end
    if i > 7
        break
    end
    println(i)
end

card: `for i in 1:5 ... end` counts from 1 to 5
`1:2:9` counts in steps of 2; `10:-1:1` counts down
`while x > 0 ... end` repeats while the condition is true
`break` leaves the loop; `continue` goes to the next round
At the top level of a script: `global total += i`

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions, use the short form f(x) = ..., give parameters default values and meet multiple dispatch.

lesson.md: A **function** gives a piece of code a name, so you can use it again and again. You write it between `function` and `end`. The names in parentheses are the **parameters**: they receive the values that you pass in when you call the function.

lesson.code:
function greet(name)
    println("Hello, $(name)!")
end

greet("Ana")
greet("Ben")

lesson.md: `return` sends a value back to the caller. Without `return`, a Julia function gives back the value of its last line.

lesson.code:
function add(a, b)
    return a + b
end

function multiply(a, b)
    a * b
end

println(add(2, 3))
println(multiply(add(1, 1), 5))

lesson.md: A function that fits on one line can use the short form: `name(parameters) = expression`. It works exactly like the long form.

lesson.code:
square(x) = x^2
is_even(n) = n % 2 == 0
println(square(6))
println(is_even(7))

lesson.md: A parameter can have a **default value**, written with `=`. When the caller leaves out that argument, Julia uses the default.

lesson.code:
function greet(name, greeting = "Hello")
    println("$greeting, $(name)!")
end

greet("Ana")
greet("Ben", "Welcome")

lesson.md: Variables that you create inside a function belong to that function. Other code cannot see them. A loop inside a function can change them without `global`.

lesson.code:
function total(n)
    s = 0
    for i in 1:n
        s += i
    end
    return s
end

println(total(4))

lesson.md: With `::` you tell Julia which type a parameter needs, for example `x::Int`. You can then define the same function name several times for different types. Each version is a **method**. Julia picks the method that fits the types of the arguments. This is called **multiple dispatch**.

lesson.code:
describe(x::Int) = "a whole number"
describe(x::String) = "some text"
describe(x::Bool) = "true or false"

println(describe(42))
println(describe("hi"))
println(describe(false))
lesson.output:
a whole number
some text
true or false

lesson.md: If no method fits, Julia stops with a `MethodError`. Here, `describe(2.5)` fails, because there is no method for `Float64`.

card: `function add(a, b) ... end`; the last value is returned

units.title: Arrays
units.summary: Keep many values in an array, add and read items, and build new arrays with comprehensions and broadcasting.

lesson.md: An **array** holds many values in a fixed order. You write it with square brackets and commas: `[10, 20, 30]`. Like strings, arrays start at index **1**: `nums[1]` is the first item and `nums[end]` the last. `length` counts the items.

lesson.code:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
println(nums)
println(nums[1])
println(nums[end])
println(length(nums))

lesson.md: You can change an item by assigning to its index: `fruits[2] = "plum"`. `push!` adds a new item at the end of the array.

lesson.code:
fruits = ["apple", "pear"]
fruits[2] = "plum"
push!(fruits, "kiwi")
println(fruits)
println(length(fruits))

lesson.md: A function name that ends in `!` tells you that the function changes its argument. `push!` changes the array itself and does not create a new one.
`sum`, `maximum` and `minimum` work on a whole array. `sort` gives a sorted copy. `x in nums` checks if the value `x` is in the array.

lesson.code:
scores = [7, 3, 9, 5]
println(sum(scores))
println(maximum(scores))
println(sort(scores))
println(9 in scores)

lesson.md: An empty array for whole numbers is written `Int[]`. You can fill it with `push!` in a loop. `push!` changes the array but does not give the name `squares` a new value, so you do not need `global` here.

lesson.code:
squares = Int[]
for i in 1:4
    push!(squares, i^2)
end
println(squares)

lesson.md: A **comprehension** builds a new array in one line: `[expression for x in sequence]`. You can add a condition with `if` at the end. Then only the values that pass the condition go into the new array.

lesson.code:
squares = [i^2 for i in 1:4]
println(squares)
evens = [n for n in 1:10 if n % 2 == 0]
println(evens)

lesson.md: A dot in front of an operator applies it to every item. This is called **broadcasting**. `nums .+ 1` adds 1 to each item, and `nums .* 2` doubles each one. A dot after a function name does the same for functions: `uppercase.(words)`.

lesson.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
println(nums .+ 1)
println(nums .* 2)
words = ["a", "b"]
println(uppercase.(words))

units.title: Dictionaries and structs
units.summary: Look up values by key in a Dict and group related data in your own types with struct.

lesson.md: A **dictionary**, or `Dict`, stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**. You write each pair as `key => value`. To get a value, put its key in square brackets.

lesson.code:
ages = Dict("Ana" => 30, "Ben" => 25)
println(ages["Ana"])
ages["Cleo"] = 41
ages["Ben"] = 26
println(ages["Ben"])
println(length(ages))

lesson.md: Assigning to a key adds a new pair, or replaces the value if the key already exists. `haskey` checks if a key exists. `get(d, key, default)` gives the default value when the key is missing.

lesson.code:
stock = Dict("apple" => 5, "pear" => 0)
println(haskey(stock, "kiwi"))
println(get(stock, "kiwi", 0))
println(get(stock, "apple", 0))

lesson.md: Reading a missing key with square brackets, like `stock["kiwi"]`, stops the program with a `KeyError`.
`keys(d)` gives all keys and `values(d)` gives all values. A dictionary keeps no fixed order. When the order matters, turn the keys into an array with `collect` and sort it with `sort`.

lesson.code:
prices = Dict("tea" => 3, "cake" => 4, "juice" => 2)
for name in sort(collect(keys(prices)))
    println("$name: $(prices[name])")
end
println(sum(values(prices)))

lesson.md: A **struct** is your own type. It groups several values, called **fields**. You list the fields between `struct` and `end`, each with its type after `::`. You create a value by calling the struct name like a function, and you read a field with a dot: `p.name`.

lesson.code:
struct Person
    name::String
    age::Int
end

p = Person("Ana", 30)
println(p.name)
println(p.age + 1)
println(p)

lesson.md: You cannot change the fields of a `struct` after you create it. If you need to change them, write `mutable struct` instead.

lesson.code:
mutable struct Counter
    count::Int
end

c = Counter(0)
c.count += 1
c.count += 1
println(c.count)

lesson.md: Your own types work with multiple dispatch. A function can have one method for each struct, and Julia picks the right one.

lesson.code:
struct Rect
    w::Int
    h::Int
end

struct Square
    side::Int
end

area(r::Rect) = r.w * r.h
area(s::Square) = s.side^2

println(area(Rect(2, 3)))
println(area(Square(4)))
